patient_information: A 31-year-old woman from Malawi, who was diagnosed with HIV two months prior following an episode of cryptococcal meningitis. She was being treated with a maintenance dose of fluconazole. One month before presentation, she began antiretroviral therapy with stavudine (d4T), lamivudine (3TC), and nevirapine (NVP), along with co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. She has no known allergies.
chief_complaint: Generalized skin rash for three days.
history_of_present_illness: The patient developed a generalized skin rash that began on her trunk three days ago and subsequently spread to her extremities and mucous membranes, including the lips, oral mucosa, conjunctivae, and genital mucosa. One day before the rash appeared, she developed a productive cough with whitish sputum. For the past two days, she has also experienced a sore throat and dysuria. The rash is non-itchy, and she has difficulty and pain with talking and eating due to swollen lips.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient resides in Malawi. Her primary exposure risk is pharmacological, having commenced a new antiretroviral regimen (stavudine, lamivudine, nevirapine) and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis one month prior to the onset of her symptoms.
vitals: Her temperature is 37.7°C (99.9°F), blood pressure is 120/68 mmHg, pulse is 90 bpm, and respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute.
physical_exam: There is a generalized, non-itchy maculopapular rash involving the skin and mucous membranes, with sparing of the palms and soles. Examination reveals bilateral conjunctivitis. The eyelids and lips are covered with haemorrhagic crusts, and the lips are swollen, making it difficult for her to open her mouth. The chest is clear on auscultation.
labs_and_diagnostics: Blood cultures and a rapid malaria test were performed upon admission and both were negative.
differential_diagnosis: The most likely diagnosis is Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS)/toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which is a potentially life-threatening mucocutaneous hypersensitivity reaction most commonly caused by drugs. The timing of the rash, appearing weeks after initiation of nevirapine and co-trimoxazole, strongly supports this diagnosis, especially given her HIV-positive status which increases the incidence. Other possibilities for the prodromal symptoms, such as a bacterial or viral infection or malaria, were less likely given the subsequent mucocutaneous eruption and negative tests.
management_and_clinical_course: Upon admission, all antiretroviral drugs and co-trimoxazole were stopped. The patient received supportive care including IV fluids, a urinary catheter, 0.9% normal saline as a mouthwash, and dexamethasone eye ointment. An NG tube was declined by the family. Her fever and cough resolved spontaneously, and she was discharged after 10 days. After all lesions had healed completely, she was successfully started on a new antiretroviral combination where nevirapine was replaced by efavirenz. Co-trimoxazole was not re-initiated. The new regimen was well tolerated without any recurrence of the rash.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis is Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), a severe mucocutaneous hypersensitivity reaction. The diagnosis was made clinically based on the characteristic generalized maculopapular rash involving skin and multiple mucosal surfaces (oral, conjunctival, genital). The condition was attributed to her recently initiated medications, with nevirapine and co-trimoxazole identified as the most likely causative agents. The diagnosis was further supported by the resolution of symptoms after withdrawal of these drugs and the absence of recurrence upon starting a different antiretroviral regimen.
